title: Are Ryobi Tools Brushless? Not All: Look for the HP Badge
description: No: many 18V ONE+ tools still use brushed motors; the HP line is brushless, like the PBLDD02 drill Ryobi rates at 850 in-lbs. How to tell and when it matters.
dek: No: many 18V ONE+ tools still use brushed motors; the HP line is brushless, like the PBLDD02 drill Ryobi rates at 850 in-lbs.
intro: Some are, many are not. Ryobi's brushless tools carry the HP badge and say brushless in the name; the cheaper ONE+ tools without it still use brushed motors, and that is fine for plenty of homeowners.

No, not all Ryobi tools are brushless. In the 18V ONE+ range, the brushless models are the ONE+ HP tools, such as the PBLDD02 drill that Ryobi rates at up to 850 in-lbs of torque; the budget ONE+ tools without the HP badge use brushed motors. The battery is the same either way. This page shows how to tell them apart and when the upgrade is worth paying for.

quickAnswer: Only some of them. Ryobi sells its 18V ONE+ tools in two tiers. The ONE+ HP tools use brushless motors, and Ryobi puts both "HP" and "Brushless" in their product names. The standard ONE+ tools, the cheapest ones in the orange aisle, mostly use brushed motors, and their names do not say brushless. Both tiers run on the same 18V ONE+ batteries. The 40V outdoor line is a separate battery system with its own brushless and brushed models.

sections.h: Are All Ryobi ONE+ Tools Brushless?

blocks.p: No. ONE+ is the name of Ryobi's 18V battery platform, not a motor type. It covers hundreds of tools, from drills and saws to inflators, fans, glue guns and string trimmers, and only part of that catalog is brushless. Ryobi built the platform around affordable brushed tools first and added brushless motors later, mostly under the ONE+ HP name. Both kinds are still on sale side by side, often on the same shelf, which is exactly why the question comes up so often.

The brushless models are concentrated where a motor works hardest: drills, impact drivers, impact wrenches, circular saws, reciprocating saws, grinders, rotary hammers and the bigger outdoor tools. Ryobi also makes compact HP versions of the drill and impact driver that are shorter and lighter than the full-size HP models. On the brushed side you will find the entry drill and impact driver, many specialty and light-duty tools, and most of the low-draw gadgets like lights, fans and speakers, where a brushless motor would add cost without adding anything you would notice.

The practical answer to "are all Ryobi ONE+ tools brushless" is this: assume a ONE+ tool is brushed unless its name or packaging says brushless. That default will be right almost every time, and it protects you from paying HP money for a basic tool that a retailer has photographed next to an HP battery.

sections.h: How Can You Tell If a Ryobi Tool Is Brushless?

blocks.p: Read the product name. Ryobi names its brushless tools plainly, for example "18V ONE+ HP Brushless 1/2 in. Drill/Driver" and "18V ONE+ HP Brushless 1/4 in. Impact Driver" on its own site. If the word brushless is missing from the full product name on ryobitools.com or the retailer listing, treat the tool as brushed. The basic PCL206 drill page, for example, describes "a powerful motor" and never calls it brushless.

blocks.h3: Look for the HP badge on the tool

blocks.p: ONE+ HP tools carry an HP mark on the housing and the packaging, and Ryobi describes the HP line as pairing brushless motors with advanced electronics and its high-performance lithium batteries. The badge is the quickest check in a store aisle or a photo of a used tool. Standard ONE+ tools carry the ONE+ logo without the HP mark.

blocks.h3: Use the model number as a hint, then confirm

blocks.p: Ryobi's current HP drill and impact model numbers start with PBL (PBLDD02 drill, PBLID01 impact driver, PBLIW01 impact wrench), while the current basic drill and impact driver start with PCL (PCL206 and PCL235). That pattern is handy, but Ryobi does not publish it as a rule, and other product families use other prefixes. Type the exact model number into ryobitools.com and read the name before you rely on it.

sections.h: Brushless vs Brushed Motor Drill: What Is the Difference?

blocks.p: A brushed motor uses small carbon brushes that rub against a spinning commutator to switch the current through the motor's windings. A brushless motor does that switching electronically, with a circuit board that reads the rotor's position and times the current itself. Nothing rubs, so less energy turns into friction and heat, and the tool's electronics can adjust power to the load. That is true of every brand, not only Ryobi.

What that gets you, in general terms: more of the battery's energy goes into turning the bit, so a brushless tool typically runs longer per charge and holds its speed better when the load goes up, such as a spade bit in a wet joist or a long lag screw. Brushless tools are often more compact for the same power, because the motor can be smaller. And there are no brushes to wear out, so one of the classic service items on a brushed tool simply disappears.

How much difference you get depends on the specific tools being compared, which is why we do not quote a runtime percentage of our own. Makers do quote figures against their own older tools. Ryobi, for example, says the HP PBLDD01 drill delivers up to 20 percent faster drilling and up to 50 percent more torque compared with its older P215 brushed drill, and that the PBLID01 impact driver's brushless motor delivers up to 25 percent faster driving. Those are Ryobi's claims, measured its own way.
THE RULE
Brushless matters most on tools that work hard for long stretches.

Drills on big bits, impact drivers on long screws, saws, grinders and trimmers gain the most. A brushed motor is perfectly adequate for a light that sips power, a glue gun, or a drill that hangs pictures twice a month.

Brushed motors still have real advantages: they cost less to build, so the tools are cheaper, and the technology is simple and proven. The brushes on a homeowner's drill can last for years of occasional use. If you own a brushed drill that works, it is not obsolete; it just has less in reserve when the job gets heavy.

sections.h: Is the Ryobi ONE+ Drill Good?

blocks.p: Yes, for household work, with the right model. The ONE+ HP brushless drill is the one we recommend. Our pillar guide names the PBLDD02 as its value pick; it is Ryobi's current full-size HP brushless drill and the successor to the PBLDD01. Ryobi rates the PBLDD02 at up to 850 in-lbs of torque with a two-speed gearbox of 0-700 and 0-2,150 RPM, a 24-position clutch and a 1/2-inch chuck, and it is sold bare or in a kit with a 4Ah battery and charger.

Ryobi now marks the bare PBLDD01 as discontinued on its site, though remaining kits can still turn up at retailers. If you find one at a good price, it remains a capable drill: Ryobi rates it at up to 750 in-lbs with 0-500 and 0-2,100 RPM and the same 24-position clutch. Both carry Ryobi's 3-year warranty. Compare what battery comes in the box, because a small 2Ah pack runs down quickly on hole saws.

The basic brushed ONE+ drill, the PCL206, is a different proposition. Ryobi rates it at up to 515 in-lbs with 0-450 and 0-1,750 RPM, and it is one of the cheapest ways into a name-brand 18V platform. Owners commonly report it is fine for furniture assembly, hanging shelves, small pilot holes and occasional deck screws. Where it struggles is sustained heavy drilling, such as large spade bits or hole saws through framing, where a brushless drill keeps its speed and the brushed one slows and warms up.

So the answer to "is the Ryobi ONE+ drill good" depends on which one. For a first drill that will see decks, fences and remodeling, spend the extra on the HP brushless model. For a drawer-and-shelf drill, or a second drill to keep a driver bit in, the brushed one is good value. Our [Ryobi tools review](/ryobi-tools-review/) covers the rest of the range in the same way: the platform is strong, but not every tool in it is.

sections.h: Are Ryobi ONE+ Impact Drivers and 1/2-Inch Impact Wrenches Brushless?

blocks.p: The HP ones are. The PBLID01 is Ryobi's ONE+ HP brushless 1/4-inch impact driver; Ryobi rates it at up to 2,200 in-lbs of torque, 0-2,900 RPM and up to 4,000 impacts per minute, with a 3-year warranty, sold as a bare tool. The basic PCL235 impact driver is the non-HP option, rated by Ryobi at up to 1,800 in-lbs and 0-2,700 RPM. An impact driver of either kind will sink deck screws and lag bolts that make a drill's clutch slip, but the brushless model has more in reserve on long structural screws.

If you are searching for Ryobi ONE+ 1/2-inch impact reviews, you are usually after an impact wrench for lug nuts and suspension bolts rather than a driver. Ryobi's top 18V model is the PBLIW01, an HP brushless 4-mode 1/2-inch high-torque impact wrench that Ryobi rates at 1,170 ft-lbs of breakaway torque and 700 ft-lbs of fastening torque. Ryobi also sells a smaller compact HP brushless 1/2-inch wrench for tighter spaces and lighter work.

Owners commonly report that the HP impact wrench handles car and light-truck lug nuts with ease, which is the job most homeowners buy it for. Two cautions apply. First, breakaway torque is a loosening figure; never use an impact wrench at full power to tighten lug nuts. Run them on snug, then finish with a [torque wrench](/best-torque-wrench/) to your vehicle's spec, or you risk stretched studs and warped rotors. Second, use impact-rated sockets only; chrome hand sockets can crack.

For impact drivers across every battery platform, including how Ryobi's HP model compares with Milwaukee, DeWalt and Makita, see our [best impact driver guide](/best-impact-driver/). Wear safety glasses with any impact tool; bits and fasteners can snap under hammering loads.

sections.h: ONE+ HP vs ONE+ vs 40V: Which Ryobi Batteries Fit Which Tools?

blocks.p: Every Ryobi 18V ONE+ battery fits every 18V ONE+ tool, HP or not. Ryobi states it directly on its product pages: any 18V ONE+ battery works with any 18V ONE+ product. That includes the HP high-performance packs, which fit the old brushed tools, and the older ONE+ packs, which fit the new HP brushless tools. This backward compatibility is the single best thing about the platform and the main reason people stay with it.

Fit is not the same as performance, though. Ryobi says its HP tools are designed to get the most from its high-performance batteries, and our [Ryobi review](/ryobi-tools-review/) notes that high-draw HP tools reach their best results on the larger HP packs. A small, old 1.5Ah pack will run an HP circular saw or impact wrench, but not for long, and it will sag under load. If you buy a high-draw HP tool, budget for at least one 4Ah or larger pack.

The 40V line is a separate system for mowers, blowers, chainsaws, snow blowers and other big outdoor tools. A 40V battery will not fit an 18V ONE+ tool, and an 18V pack will not fit a 40V tool. The 40V HP models are brushless, and as with the 18V side, Ryobi puts HP and brushless in the names, so the same reading-the-name rule applies. If you need both, plan for two chargers and two battery families.

sections.h: Is Ryobi ONE Plus Good, and When Is a Brushed Tool Fine?

blocks.p: Ryobi ONE+ is a good platform for homeowners and a weaker one for daily professional use. The range is enormous, the batteries are cheap and backward compatible, and the HP brushless drills, impact drivers and saws are strong enough for decks, fences, furniture builds and most remodeling. Where Ryobi falls behind Milwaukee, DeWalt and Makita is durability under daily jobsite abuse, the top end of power, and the feel of the trigger and clutch on the basic tools. If you are deciding between the pro brands instead, read [Milwaukee vs DeWalt](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/).

A brushed ONE+ tool is a perfectly sensible buy in several cases. If the tool runs for a few minutes at a time, such as a light, a fan, an inflator, a glue gun or a hand vacuum, a brushless motor adds cost you will never notice. If it is a second drill that will hold a driver bit while the HP drill holds a drill bit, brushed is fine. And if the budget is tight, a brushed drill now beats an HP drill you put off buying for a year.

Spend on HP brushless where the motor works hard and long: the main drill, the impact driver, the circular and reciprocating saws, the grinder, and the string trimmer. Those are the tools where owners commonly report the clearest difference, and where a brushed motor is most likely to bog down, heat up and wear its brushes. The price gap between the brushed and HP versions of these tools is usually modest compared with the life you get from them.

mistakes: Assuming Every ONE+ Tool Is Brushless

ONE+ is the battery platform, not the motor. Most of the cheapest ONE+ tools are brushed, and the brushless ones say HP and brushless in the name. If the listing does not say brushless, assume it is brushed and price it accordingly before you compare it with an HP kit.
Trusting the Battery in the Photo

An HP battery fitted to a basic tool in a product photo or a used listing does not make the tool brushless. Check the badge and the model number on the tool itself, then look it up on ryobitools.com. Sellers often pair the best battery they own with whatever tool they are selling.
Comparing Ryobi Torque Numbers With Other Brands

Ryobi's in-lbs ratings come from its own test method, and Milwaukee, DeWalt and Makita each use theirs. A higher number on a Ryobi box does not prove it out-twists a pro drill. Use the ratings to compare Ryobi tools with each other and read owner reports for the rest.
Running HP Tools on Tiny Old Packs

Old 1.5Ah ONE+ batteries fit HP brushless tools, but they cannot feed a saw or an impact wrench for long, and power sags under load. Owners who call an HP tool weak are often running it on the smallest pack they own. Add at least one 4Ah or larger pack for high-draw tools.
Tightening Lug Nuts With the Impact Wrench

A brushless 1/2-inch impact wrench is rated for far more torque than a wheel needs. Running lug nuts down at full power can stretch studs and warp rotors. Snug them with the impact, or by hand, then finish with a torque wrench set to the figure in your owner's manual.
bottomLine: Not all Ryobi tools are brushless. In the 18V ONE+ range, the brushless tools are the ONE+ HP models, and Ryobi names them as brushless; the basic ONE+ tools without the HP badge use brushed motors. Every ONE+ battery fits every ONE+ tool either way, while the 40V outdoor line is a separate system. Buy the HP brushless version of the tools that work hard, starting with the drill and impact driver, and save money with brushed tools for light, occasional jobs. Check the name and model number on ryobitools.com before you pay HP prices, and pair high-draw tools with a larger battery.

faqs.q: Are all Ryobi ONE+ tools brushless?
faqs.a: No. ONE+ is Ryobi's 18V battery platform, and it includes both brushed and brushless tools. The brushless models are mostly sold as ONE+ HP and say brushless in the product name. The budget ONE+ drill, impact driver and many light-duty tools use brushed motors. All of them take the same 18V ONE+ batteries.

faqs.q: Is Ryobi ONE+ HP always brushless?
faqs.a: Ryobi describes its ONE+ HP line as combining brushless motors with advanced electronics and high-performance batteries, and its HP tools are named as brushless on its site. If you see the HP badge on a current Ryobi tool, it is a brushless model. Still confirm the exact model number on ryobitools.com if you are buying used or from a third-party seller.

faqs.q: Do ONE+ HP tools work with old Ryobi batteries?
faqs.a: Yes. Ryobi states that any 18V ONE+ battery works with any 18V ONE+ product, so older packs fit the HP brushless tools. They will not deliver the tool's best performance on high-draw jobs, though. Ryobi says HP tools are built to get the most from its high-performance packs, so pair saws and impact wrenches with a larger pack.

faqs.q: Is a brushless drill worth it for a homeowner?
faqs.a: For a main drill that will see decks, fences, hole saws and remodeling, yes; brushless typically gives more runtime per charge, holds speed under load and has no brushes to wear out. For light jobs like hanging pictures and assembling furniture, a brushed drill does the work for less money. Many homeowners own one of each.

faqs.q: Can you replace the brushes on a Ryobi brushed drill?
faqs.a: On many brushed tools the carbon brushes are a wear part that a service center can replace, but on budget cordless tools the repair often costs close to a new bare tool. For a homeowner's drill, the brushes usually outlast the battery and the chuck under occasional use. If a brushed drill sparks heavily or loses power, check it under the 3-year warranty first.

faqs.q: Do Ryobi 40V batteries fit ONE+ tools?
faqs.a: No. Ryobi's 40V outdoor line uses its own batteries, which do not fit 18V ONE+ tools, and 18V packs do not fit 40V tools. The 40V range includes brushless HP models and some brushed ones, and like the 18V tools, the brushless 40V models say so in the product name. Plan for two chargers if you own both.

faqs.q: Is Ryobi ONE+ good compared with Milwaukee or DeWalt?
faqs.a: For homeowners, Ryobi ONE+ HP brushless tools are good value and handle most household projects. Milwaukee and DeWalt cost more and are built for daily jobsite use, with more power at the top end and tougher housings. If you work with tools for a living, a pro brand is the better long-term platform; for weekend projects, Ryobi is enough.
